name: ground_b
prompt:
Two images are attached. The first is a layout: 12 equal squares in a 4×3 grid on a flat magenta background. The second shows finished art from the same top-down 2D city game: roofs and cars, and on the right a square of the game's old grass. Match that art's look: crisp hand-painted game art, clean confident brushwork, every small shape sharp and readable, saturated but natural colours. It must NOT look like a photograph: no blur, no photographic noise, no soft mush.

Make one image with exactly the same 4×3 layout as the first image. Fill each square with the patch of ground described for that cell below: a ground texture the game repeats over large areas under the roofs and cars.

Shape comes first:
- Each square is filled edge to edge, right into all four corners, and stops exactly at its outline. Paint over the outline itself: the finished square has no border, frame, rim, bevel, outline, shadow or vignette, and its edges are as bright and as busy as its middle.
- Draw nothing outside the squares. Outside them, keep the background fully transparent. No text, numbers, labels or grid lines anywhere.

Rules for every cell:
- Look straight down (orthographic). No perspective, no horizon, no light falling off towards any edge.
- Each square is 9.2 × 9.2 m of ground. Keep everything true to size: a grass blade a few centimetres, a daisy or clover leaf the size of a coin, a ripple a few tens of centimetres.
- No direction and no pattern: blades, flowers and ripples point every way at once, scattered at random, never in rows, stripes, lines or a grid, so the texture looks the same turned any way.
- Even texture: the same tone and the same density of small detail all over the square, with no single large feature, blotch, path, puddle, shadow or object.
- Squares that share a description are the same ground: draw them in exactly the same colours, density and style, as different patches of one lawn or one river, so they can be joined without a visible seam.
- Nothing stands on the ground: no trees, bushes, rocks, litter, cars, people, kerbs, markings or lines.

Cells, left to right, top to bottom:

Row 1 — cells 1, 2, 3, 4: a kept town lawn: fresh mid green, dense short painted blades in a few greens with lighter tips, a little scattered clover and a very few tiny white daisies.

Row 2 — cells 5, 6, 7, 8: a worn, drier town lawn: yellow-green and olive painted blades, thinner, with tiny scattered spots of bare brown earth and a few tiny yellow flowers. The same style as row 1, clearly the same grass, only drier and more worn.

Row 3 — cells 9 and 10: still river water: deep blue-green, small soft painted ripples a few tens of centimetres across, curving every way, a very few small pale glints.
Row 3 — cells 11 and 12: livelier river water: the same deep blue-green a touch lighter and greener, more broken small ripples curving every way, more small pale glints.
